title: Salman Khan and Farhan Akhtar Are Quietly Plotting a Two-Part Period Epic. The Subject Is One of India's Most Iconic Figures.
excerpt: After signing a superhero comedy with Raj & DK, Bhai is chasing his biggest swing yet — a grand historical action saga under Excel Entertainment, told across two films. Cameras could roll in summer 2027.
body:
Picture **Salman Khan** — not in a torn shirt flexing for a Friday crowd, but armoured, on horseback, leading a battle that India still tells stories about. That is the image the industry is whispering about this week, and for once the whisper is loud enough to feel real.

According to an exclusive from **Pinkvilla**, Salman Khan is in active talks with actor-filmmaker **Farhan Akhtar** for a large-scale historical action drama — a grand period saga based on one of the most celebrated figures in Indian history, mounted to unfold across **two films**. If it lands, it would be the first time these two have ever shared a project, and arguably the most ambitious undertaking of Salman's three-decade career.

> "It is a massive period action drama mounted on a grand scale. The idea is to tell the story across 2 films." — a source close to the project, to Pinkvilla

The contours are still soft. Sources stress the talks are early — Salman and Farhan have reportedly been meeting regularly for over a month, but nothing has reached the paperwork stage. What's clear is the temperature in the room. "Salman has loved what he's heard so far and has shown keen interest," the insider said. Both camps are described as excited about the possibility of finally coming together. A clearer picture is expected by the end of the year, with production tentatively eyed for the **summer of 2027**.

Here's the detail that makes this more than gossip: the project would be produced under **Excel Entertainment**, the banner Farhan runs with **Ritesh Sidhwani** — the house behind *Dil Chahta Hai*, *Don*, *Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara*, and Farhan's own freshly released war drama *120 Bahadur*. Excel knows how to mount scale with taste. Pair that production muscle with Salman's raw mass pull, and you have a combination Bollywood hasn't quite tried before.

The two-part structure is the most telling choice of all. This is the **Baahubali** template, and the industry has watched it work over and over — a story so big it refuses to fit in one sitting, engineered to leave a billion people asking a question they'll pay twice to answer. *Baahubali: The Conclusion* sold over 100 million tickets in India alone and rewrote the box-office record book. *KGF*, *Pushpa*, *Dhurandhar* — the second instalment has become the place where Indian franchises turn into phenomena. To design a Salman Khan vehicle in two parts from the jump is to bet, openly, on legend-making.

It also marks a fascinating pivot for **Bhai**. For years the knock on Salman was that he coasted — charisma over craft, the same swagger on loop. But look at the slate he's assembling now. He's already signed an action-comedy with **Raj Nidimoru and Krishna D.K.**, the *Family Man* duo, playing a retiring superhero. He's shooting an untitled film with director **Vamshi Paidipally** opposite **Nayanthara**. And now a period epic with Farhan Akhtar. This is a superstar reaching, deliberately, for material with weight — the kind of roles that outlive a weekend's collections.

Farhan, for his part, is having a moment of his own. *120 Bahadur*, his retelling of the 1962 Battle of Rezang La in which Major Shaitan Singh Bhati led 120 soldiers against thousands, drew praise across the industry — including, fittingly, from Salman himself, who lauded its trailer. A filmmaker fluent in patriotic spectacle, meeting a star who can fill any theatre in the country. The logic almost writes itself.

Who is the "iconic figure" at the centre of it all? That's the question nobody will answer yet, and the speculation is half the fun. A warrior king? A freedom fighter? A historical commander whose name still stirs a room? Whatever the answer, casting Salman Khan in the lead guarantees it arrives wrapped in event-scale anticipation.

For the diaspora, a Salman period epic is the kind of release that turns a multiplex in Edison or Wembley or Mississauga into a homecoming — first-day-first-show, family in tow, the whole row chanting. Two-part epics are practically built for the NRI audience, who treat these films as cultural appointments, not casual outings. If Excel mounts this the way it mounts everything, expect a global theatrical rollout in multiple languages when the time comes.

For now, it's a handshake that hasn't happened yet and a story nobody's confirmed the name of. But the shape of it — Bhai, armoured, leading an army across two films under a prestige banner — is exactly the kind of swing that, win or lose, makes Bollywood worth watching. Watch this space toward the end of the year.
